sysd-reliab-051.title: Kubernetes control plane: the brain behind the API
sysd-reliab-051.text: Every operation on pods goes through one door: the API server. The Kubernetes control plane manages the cluster's workload and its worker nodes and directs communication across the system. In production it usually runs across multiple computers for fault tolerance and high availability. The API server serves the Kubernetes API using JSON over HTTPS as both the internal and external interface. It processes and validates REST requests (see {{ref:sysd-msg-002}}) and updates the state of API objects in the key-value store that backs all cluster data (see {{ref:sysd-reliab-052}}). The scheduler selects the node an unscheduled pod runs on, based on resource availability and other constraints. It tracks allocation so workload is not scheduled beyond a node's available resources. The controller manager runs the controllers, including the node, job, EndpointSlice and ServiceAccount controllers, as a single process. Kubernetes follows a primary/replica architecture, with components divided between those that manage an individual node and those that form the control plane.

sysd-reliab-053.title: Kubernetes controllers: loops that keep reality matching the declaration
sysd-reliab-053.text: Declare three instances of a pod, and a controller notices when only two are running. A Kubernetes controller is a reconciliation loop that drives the actual cluster state toward the desired state by creating, updating and deleting the resources it manages. Objects record the desired state in a spec field, while the controller of the resource keeps a status field describing the current state up to date. In the example, the Deployment controller finds two running and schedules the creation of another. The ReplicaSet controller runs a specified number of copies of a pod across the cluster and creates replacement pods if the underlying node fails. The DaemonSet controller ensures a pod runs on every node, which suits workloads tied to the host such as log collection and storage services. The Job controller runs pods to completion, as in a batch job. Label selectors often specify the set of pods a controller manages. The controller manager is one process managing several core controllers, and custom controllers can be installed to extend Kubernetes together with custom resources.

sysd-reliab-158.title: Pod templates: the blueprint a controller copies from
sysd-reliab-158.text: Change a pod template and nothing happens to the Pods already running. A pod template is the specification a workload controller uses to create the Pods it manages. Controllers for workload resources such as Deployments, Jobs and DaemonSets create Pods from a template included in the workload object. The template is part of the workload's desired state. Changing it has no direct effect on existing Pods. The controller creates replacement Pods from the new template instead of patching the old ones, until all old Pods are replaced. A running Pod can be edited in place only a little, since most metadata is immutable.

sysd-reliab-062.title: Kubernetes operators: a human operator's knowledge, automated
sysd-reliab-062.text: Some applications need a human who knows how to run them. A Kubernetes Operator captures that knowledge and automates it, for example taking and restoring backups or handling upgrades together with schema or configuration changes. It is the combination of custom resources and custom controllers. The Kubernetes API can be extended with Custom Resources, declared through Custom Resource Definitions that can be registered and unregistered without restarting a running cluster. Custom controllers observe those resources and reconcile the cluster toward the declared desired state, giving users a declarative API.

sysd-reliab-052.title: etcd: the cluster's memory, and why it picks consistency
sysd-reliab-052.text: During a network partition, etcd favors consistency over availability, because consistency is crucial for correctly scheduling and operating services. That is the CAP trade-off ({{ref:sysd-scale-107}}) made on purpose. etcd is a persistent, lightweight, distributed key-value data store, originally developed as part of CoreOS. In Kubernetes it is the backing store for all cluster data. It reliably holds the cluster's configuration, and so represents the overall state of the cluster at any given point in time. The API server uses its watch API to monitor the cluster and roll out critical configuration changes. It also restores any divergence back to the desired state declared there.

sysd-reliab-154.title: Ingress controllers and classes: who carries out the rules
sysd-reliab-154.text: Ingress controllers should all fit the reference specification, but in reality they operate slightly differently. An Ingress controller carries out the Ingress rules, and one must be running to satisfy an Ingress. Ingresses can be implemented by different controllers, so each should name an IngressClass. That resource carries extra configuration, including the name of the controller that implements the class. An IngressClass can reference a parameters resource, cluster-scoped by default or namespaced. Namespaced parameters let the cluster operator delegate control of settings such as load balancer configuration to a workload's team.

sysd-reliab-141.title: Feature toggle: shipping unfinished code hidden behind a switch
sysd-reliab-141.text: A feature toggle lets unfinished code ship hidden. It is a condition in the code that enables or disables a feature at runtime, as an alternative to maintaining multiple feature branches. Toggles are also called feature flags, switches or gates. An unfinished feature can be merged into the main branch and hidden behind a toggle. It can then be switched on in a test environment, or in production on demand for some or all users. That shortens integration cycles and allows many small incremental versions, so releasing often becomes easier. Toggles come as release, experiment, ops and permissioning types, which differ by how long they should live. An ops toggle can act as a kill switch that disables a feature at runtime during an incident. Toggle debt arises when a feature is toggled on permanently and dead code remains, so toggles need lifecycle management. Martin Fowler says a release toggle should be your last choice; it is better to break the feature into smaller parts that can each be released safely.

sysd-reliab-166.title: Configuration distribution models: four ways to get settings to a running service
sysd-reliab-166.text:
Configuration changes are a potential source of instability, so every distribution scheme stores configuration in the main source repository and enforces strict code review. The schemes differ in how they trade flexibility, simplicity and drift between the stored and the running version.

Mainline: changes to configuration files at the head of the main branch are reviewed and then applied to the running system. This decouples binary releases from configuration, but the running version can skew from the checked-in one. Same package: shipping configuration files in the binary's package binds the two tightly and limits flexibility, but simplifies deployment because only one package is installed.

Separate configuration packages: snapshotting configuration alongside its binary lets each change independently. A wrong feature flag value can then be fixed by cherry picking, rebuilding the configuration package and deploying, without a new binary. External store: configuration that must change often or while the binary is running can be read from an external store such as Chubby, Bigtable or a source-based filesystem. Project owners weigh these options and choose case by case.

sysd-reliab-039.title: Blue-green deployment: swap environments, roll back by swapping again
sysd-reliab-039.text: Blue-green deployment makes a release a switch, and a rollback the same switch in reverse. Two servers or environments are kept, one blue and one green. Only one handles requests at a time, for example the one DNS (see {{ref:sysd-found-101}}) points to, while the other is a staging server on a private network. Changes are installed on the non-live environment and tested through the private network; once verified, it is swapped with the live one and the changes go live. Because requests move instantly from one environment to the other, ideally no request goes unfulfilled, so downtime is reduced. Rollback is quick: traffic is simply routed back to the previous live environment, which never received the deployed changes. The cost is running two environments at once, and duplicate infrastructure, even temporarily, can be prohibitive for smaller organizations. Complex database migrations are harder, since blue and green must hold consistent data; migration tools that keep both environments backward compatible are a common solution. Blue-green is often contrasted with {{ref:sysd-reliab-142}} and suits high-stake updates.

sysd-reliab-040.title: Deployment strategies: recreate, rolling, blue-green, canary, shadow and A/B
sysd-reliab-040.text: There is more than one way to replace a running version of an application with a new one, and each manages the update differently. Recreate terminates all existing instances at once and then creates new ones with the updated version; it suits non-critical applications or early development. A rolling update replaces instances one by one, keeping availability high during the process, and suits periodic releases. Blue-green keeps two identical environments, one with the current version and one with the updated version, and switches traffic from blue to the prepared green environment. A canary sends the new version to a subset of users or servers for testing before broader deployment, to validate its impact on that subset. Shadow deployment redirects a copy of live traffic to the new version so it can be tested without affecting production users. It is the most complex strategy, because it needs mock services that interact with the new version. A/B testing runs several versions at once on different users to compare performance or user experience, so it aims at optimizing user experience. Another list of the most-used strategies names big bang, rolling, blue-green, canary and feature toggle deployment.

sysd-reliab-142.title: Canary release: trying a new version on a small slice of users
sysd-reliab-142.text: Turn a feature on for 1% of users and leave everyone else off: that is a canary release. It exposes a new version or feature to a small set of users first, so it can be tested incrementally before a wider rollout. The canary validates the version's impact, and if the feature's performance is not satisfactory it can be rolled back without adverse effects. Blue-green deployment is often contrasted with it. Feature flags are an alternative way to run canary launches and allow targeting by geographic location or by user attributes. The SRE book calls it a best practice to test a new release on a small subset of a typical workload. The open questions are how long to wait and how big the canary should be. In Google's release process, a typical canary deployment starts a few jobs in the production environment after system tests complete. In Kubernetes a canary is done with multiple Deployments, one per release, and a release_track label with values such as canary and production tells pods apart.

sysd-reliab-167.title: Risk-based rollouts: pushing as carefully as the service demands
sysd-reliab-167.text: A rollout should be as careful as the service is sensitive. A risk-based rollout fits how fast and how widely a release is pushed to the risk profile of the service. In development or pre-production, builds can run hourly and be pushed automatically when all tests pass. For large user-facing services, a push starts in one cluster and expands exponentially until all clusters are updated. For sensitive infrastructure, the rollout may stretch over several days, interleaving instances in different geographic regions. Automation can update all jobs at once or roll a new binary out to successive clusters over hours.

reviews.containers-orchestration-and-deployment: This chapter followed an application from isolation to release. Chroot, namespaces and cgroups let the kernel give a container its own view and its own budget, and Docker packages the result into images pulled from registries. Kubernetes then runs those containers as pods on nodes, with services, labels and Ingress routing traffic to them, probes judging their health, and a control plane of controllers steering the cluster toward the declared state. Around that sit the practices that deliver change safely: continuous delivery, release pipelines, rolling updates, blue-green and canary releases, each trading speed against risk. Virtual machines show the older way of sharing a server, which containers lighten by sharing the kernel.
